description: We’re a team of developers and creators with experience in 4+ hackathons, winning 3, Taranga 1.0, DeerHack 2026, and LUMBINIX. We enjoy building, experimenting, and solving problems. This time, we’re excited to explore NASA data and build something meaningful. We’re looking forward.
summary:
Orbit Ranger is a 3D game that lets students fly a space mission instead of just reading about one. It is made for ages seven and up and runs in a browser on a phone or laptop.

Players go through six levels. They meet a rocket and learn its parts, build it, launch it, and reach orbit. Then they design a satellite that watches for wildfires, and finally they land and walk on the Moon. Along the way they have to balance money, weight, power and data, and every choice changes how the mission ends. Up to four players can work as a crew.

The game uses real NASA data: wildfires recorded by NASA satellites, NASA images of Earth, real ground stations and real engine numbers. Any hard word can be tapped for a simple explanation, read aloud.

It matters because space is hard to learn from a textbook, where nothing moves and nothing can fail. In Orbit Ranger, students learn by doing.
details:
What it does

Orbit Ranger is a 3D game where students fly a full space mission, step by step. There are six levels. You meet a rocket and x-ray its parts, build it by dragging on tanks, engines and boosters, launch it, and steer it into orbit. Then you design a satellite that watches for wildfires and run it for three years. In the last level you plan a Moon landing, fly behind the Moon with no radio signal, land, and walk on the surface.

Every level has real trade-offs. A bigger tank holds more fuel but is heavier. A sharper camera costs more money and power. There is no single right answer, and when something fails, a short cartoon shows why and suggests one thing to try.

How it helps students learn

Any hard word in the game can be tapped. A card opens with a simple meaning, why it matters right now, and a real number. There are 111 of these words, and the game can read them aloud. A guide character called Pip gives short hints. Students also earn badges and collect cards of real NASA missions.

Benefits and impact

Space is hard to learn from a textbook, where nothing moves and nothing can fail. We want a ten-year-old with only a phone to be able to build, launch and land a mission, and remember it. The game runs in a browser on a phone or laptop, needs nothing installed, and can work offline, so it suits schools with slow internet. Up to four players can play as a crew, each with their own job, so it also works in a classroom.

NASA data

The wildfires are real fires recorded by NASA’s MODIS instruments (NASA FIRMS). The Earth images come from NASA GIBS. The ground stations are NASA’s real Near Space Network stations. The rocket uses real RS-25 engine numbers, the Moon level uses Apollo figures and landing sites, and the hangar holds 310 models from NASA 3D Resources. Prices and scores are simplified for teaching.

Tools we used

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with three.js for the 3D graphics and the Web Audio API for sound. A small Node.js server with WebSockets handles online crew play. Python and Node scripts prepare the NASA data and 3D models. The guide’s voice was recorded with an AI speech model (Higgsfield), and we used an AI coding assistant (Claude) during development.

What makes it creative

It teaches like a language app, in small steps with instant feedback, but the subject is rocket science. The rocket you build in level 2 is the one you fly in levels 3 and 4. Every 3D scene is built in code, and players can plant a flag on the Moon.

What we considered

Young players, so short sentences and pictures before text. Phones and touch screens, so drag-and-drop works with a finger. Accessibility, so the levels can be played from a keyboard and text is read aloud. Honesty, so we say clearly which numbers are real NASA data and which are simplified. And fun, because a student who enjoys the mission will remember it.
